extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and scientifically literate general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Narrative analysis of bird courtship, variability, and secondary sexual characters; discusses observational evidence, classification of variation, and causal inferences regarding sexual selection and ornament formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of female mate choice
rubrics_metrics.description: We can judge of choice being exerted only by analogy; females pursued by many males and then showing a 'marked preference' indicate deliberate mate choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated, careful observations (e.g., Audubon's accounts) showing multiple males courting and a female accepting one to infer female choice. Prefer evidence of pursuit by many males, displays, and a distinct, consistent acceptance of one male.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize observations (wild vs domesticated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviours observed in domesticated/confined birds may be vitiated by high feeding and artificial conditions and so may not reflect natural preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between captive/domesticated cases and observations in nature. Give greater weight to well-documented wild observations; treat captive anecdotes with caution, considering possible altered instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required for sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: If males display ornaments, voices, or antics and certain males are consistently accepted by females, it supports the hypothesis that female preference drove the acquisition of these characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for correlation between male ornamentation/behaviour and mating success. Examples: peacock train displays, Argus pheasant wing-feather displays, goldfinch wing-showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of variability and inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Variability and inheritance are the foundations for the work of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of selection require evidence that the traits vary among individuals and that beneficial variants are heritable; document both variation and heritability before invoking selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of variation (spontaneous vs environment-driven)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations may be divided into (a) those appearing spontaneously and (b) those directly related to surrounding conditions, affecting many individuals similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify observed differences by whether they are widespread and environmentally correlated (e.g., geographic clines) or occur sporadically in individuals; this classification affects their plausibility as raw material for sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider rarity and preservation likelihood of large deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden and strongly marked variations are rare, and even if beneficial, their preservation through natural selection depends on chance and is unlikely compared with selection on small, common differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of hypotheses that rely on single, large mutations becoming fixed; favor explanations invoking incremental, frequently occurring individual differences that selection can act upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming sexual selection without considering inheritance patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sometimes difficult to decide whether slight sexual differences arose by sexually-limited inheritance alone or have been augmented by sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate alternative mechanisms (sex-limited expression, correlated development, direct natural selection) before attributing a trait to sexual selection; seek evidence of female preference or differential mating success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlated development and pleiotropy as explanatory mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: On the principle of correlated development, a change in one part (e.g., male neck hackles) may be correlated with changes elsewhere (e.g., head feathers), explaining matched ornaments across body regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting suites of characters, consider developmental/constitutional correlations that could produce multiple co-varying traits without separate selective explanations for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry and feather structure constrain pattern formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of each feather generally causes colouring changes to be symmetrical; shaft position and feather structure often determine tint distribution, producing regular zones and symmetric markings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feather microstructure and developmental constraints to explain symmetric markings and repeating patterns (laced, spangled, pencilled feathers) rather than invoking selection for symmetry alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual origin of complex markings (ocelli) supported by intermediate forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ocelli and other complex markings show numerous gradations (e.g., minute spot → fully developed ocellus) in groups such as Lepidoptera and butterflies, suggesting a gradual evolutionary origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek series of specimens exhibiting intermediate stages in ocellus number/size; instability of ocelli in some groups supports their evolution by small incremental changes rather than sudden creation.
